## Your goal before the first class

::: {.key-idea}
Your own computer can run the course script and open its notebook.
:::

You are ready when:

1. The course environment runs **Python 3.12**.
2. The setup checker reports **`SETUP CHECK PASSED`**.
3. The notebook runs from a fresh start and reports saving **200**.
4. Codex opens the course folder and can explain the starter calculation.

::: {.notes}
This is a practical completion check, not a programming assessment. Students
should bring the working laptop to class. A later slide provides a concise
help request if one of these checks fails. Different patch versions are fine.
:::

## The tools and what they do

| Tool | Purpose | How you get it |
|---|---|---|
| Miniforge / Conda | Install and select a course environment | Install once |
| Python + packages | Run calculations and work with data | Course environment file |
| JupyterLab | Open notebooks and edit code in a browser | Course environment file |
| Git | Save versions of your work | Operating-system installer |
| GitHub account | Work with repositories online | Sign up in your browser |
| Codex | Help read, change and check project code | Desktop app or editor extension |

::: {.notes}
The recommended new Conda installation is Miniforge, which uses conda-forge.
A working Miniconda or Anaconda installation can be reused. JupyterLab supplies
an editor and terminal as well as notebooks, so a separate editor is not a
prerequisite for the desktop route. Quarto is an authoring tool and is excluded
from the student environment. Codex is the selected coding agent.
:::

## Read this once before installing

- Use your **laptop or desktop**, with an internet connection.
- Save your work and allow time for downloads and setup help.
- If Conda is already installed, first try `conda --version`.
- Follow **one operating-system route**, then the common steps.

::: {.definition}
Type one command per line. Press **Enter**, then wait for it to finish.
:::

::: {.notes}
Installation duration depends on hardware, connection and cached packages. Do
not promise a fixed runtime. Students with a functioning Conda installation
should avoid adding a second one. Terminal prompts such as (base), $, and >
are not part of the commands shown. A phone can display this guide but cannot
perform the local laptop setup used in class.
:::

## Choose your route

| Your computer | Conda installer | Where to type commands |
|---|---|---|
| Windows, Intel / AMD 64-bit | Miniforge for Windows x86_64 | Miniforge Prompt |
| Mac with an Apple chip | Miniforge for macOS arm64 | Terminal |
| Mac with an Intel processor | Miniforge for macOS x86_64 | Terminal |
| Linux | Miniforge for your architecture | Terminal |

Follow the next slides for **your** computer, then join at **“Check Conda”**.

::: {.notes}
Mac: Apple menu > About This Mac identifies an Apple chip versus an Intel
processor. Windows: Settings > System > About identifies the system type. The
listed Miniforge Windows installer is x86_64; a student with Windows on ARM
should ask the instructor to confirm their route. Native Windows is sufficient
for this course; students do not need to set up WSL to follow this guide.
Sources: https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge#requirements-and-installers
and https://support.apple.com/en-us/116943.
:::

## Windows · Install Miniforge

1. Download the [official Windows installer](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Windows-x86_64.exe).
2. Run the `.exe` file and choose installation for your own user account.
3. Keep the **Start menu shortcut** enabled.
4. Leave **Add Miniforge to PATH** unchecked; complete installation.

::: {.key-idea}
Use **Miniforge Prompt** for the commands in this guide.
:::

::: {.notes}
This route is for Windows x86_64. The file is Miniforge3-Windows-x86_64.exe.
Read and follow the installer prompts, including the licence and location.
Miniforge's documented default Windows workflow is its Start menu prompt;
global PATH editing is unnecessary. If an installer cannot use the chosen
location, record the error and ask for help instead of trying several installs.
Official instructions: https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge#windows.
:::

## Windows · Open the correct prompt

1. Open the **Start menu**.
2. Search for **Miniforge Prompt** and open it.
3. Enter:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
conda --version
```

::: {.answer}
A version number should appear. Continue at **“Check Conda”**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Miniforge Prompt is a command window prepared for Conda. A normal Command
Prompt, PowerShell window or Git Bash session may not know Conda yet. Do not
ask students to change global shell configuration when the supplied prompt
already works. Students reusing Miniconda or Anaconda may use its corresponding
prepared prompt. Source: https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge#usage.
:::

## macOS · Match the installer to your chip

Open **Apple menu → About This Mac**.

| What it shows | Download this terminal installer |
|---|---|
| Chip: Apple M-series | [Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh) |
| Processor: Intel | [Miniforge3-MacOSX-x86_64.sh](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-MacOSX-x86_64.sh) |

Open **Terminal** using Spotlight or Applications → Utilities.

::: {.notes}
Use the chip description, not the laptop's purchase date. Choose the .sh
installer linked on the slide. The next slide assumes it is in Downloads with
its original filename. Apple describes the Chip versus Processor fields at
https://support.apple.com/en-us/116943. Installer names are from
https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge#requirements-and-installers.
:::

## macOS · Run your downloaded installer

**Apple chip:**

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
bash ~/Downloads/Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh
```

**Intel processor:**

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
bash ~/Downloads/Miniforge3-MacOSX-x86_64.sh
```

Run **one** of these. Follow the prompts and accept shell initialization.
Close and reopen Terminal, then continue at **“Check Conda”**.

::: {.notes}
Read the licence and installation prompts and use the path actually downloaded.
If the browser renamed the file or used another location, adjust that path.
The interactive installer offers Conda shell initialization; accepting it
allows activation after reopening Terminal. A .sh file is run by bash, rather
than opened as a notebook. Source:
https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge#unix-like-platforms-macos-linux--wsl.
:::

## Linux · Download and run the matching installer

Check the processor architecture:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
uname -m
```

- `x86_64`: [download the x86_64 installer](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh).
- `aarch64`: [download the aarch64 installer](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-Linux-aarch64.sh).

For the x86_64 download:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
bash ~/Downloads/Miniforge3-Linux-x86_64.sh
```

Accept shell initialization, then reopen Terminal.

::: {.notes}
For aarch64, substitute the matching downloaded filename in the bash command.
If uname reports something else or the installer reports an unsupported system,
ask for help with that specific architecture. These instructions assume the
standard Downloads location. Source:
https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge#requirements-and-installers.
:::

## Check Conda · Everyone joins here

Use Miniforge Prompt on Windows, or Terminal on macOS / Linux:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
conda --version
conda env list
```

::: {.key-idea}
You should see a Conda version and a list containing **`base`**.
:::

We will create a separate environment called **`research-methods`**.

::: {.notes}
An environment is a named collection of Python and packages. The base
environment's Python version need not be 3.12: the course environment controls
our Python version. A working existing Miniconda/Anaconda installation is
sufficient here. The list may already contain other projects; keep them.
Source: https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/stable/user-guide/tasks/manage-environments.html.
:::

## Windows · Install Git

1. Open the [official Git for Windows download page](https://git-scm.com/install/windows).
2. Download and run the installer matching your computer.
3. Keep Git available from the command line and other applications.
4. Close and reopen **Miniforge Prompt** after installation.

Check:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
git --version
```

::: {.notes}
Use Git's official maintained installer. Its command-line access option makes
git available in the prompt used for the Python workflow. Reopening matters
because an existing terminal may retain the old PATH. If the check still fails,
record it for setup help. Git installation and GitHub account creation are
separate. Source: https://git-scm.com/install/windows.
:::

## macOS / Linux · Install Git

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

### macOS

If Git is missing, install Apple's command-line tools:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
xcode-select --install
```

Finish the installation dialog.

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Ubuntu / Debian

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git
```

Other distributions: [Git's Linux instructions](https://git-scm.com/install/linux).

:::
:::

Then run **`git --version`**. A version number means the check passed.

::: {.notes}
First run git --version; reuse a working installation. On macOS the Apple
installer may take some time. On Linux sudo may ask for the user's password;
terminal password entry usually shows no characters. This command requires
normal administrative installation rights. If they are unavailable on a managed
laptop, ask the institution for help. Sources: https://git-scm.com/install/mac
and https://git-scm.com/install/linux.
:::

## Create or check your GitHub account

1. Open [github.com/signup](https://github.com/signup), or sign into an existing account.
2. Complete the email verification requested by GitHub.
3. Check that you can sign in before class.

::: {.definition}
**Git** saves versions on your computer. **GitHub** hosts repositories online.
:::

We will set up commits and repository authentication in class.

::: {.notes}
The current official instructions allow a free personal account with a verified
email address. Students do not need to buy a plan for the core course workflow.
Do not ask them to create access tokens, configure SSH keys, or publish a test
repository just to complete installation. Account instructions:
https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/account-management/creating-an-account-on-github.
:::

## Get the student project files

1. [Download the student starter project](downloads/research-methods-student-kit.zip) with the code and data.
2. **Extract** it into a folder you can find again.
3. Open the extracted **`research-methods`** folder.

::: {.key-idea}
Find **`environment-student.yml`** inside that folder before continuing.
:::

Keep the code, notebook and data folders together.

::: {.notes}
The download contains the runtime files; the slides remain online. On Windows
use Extract All in File Explorer; on macOS the normal
ZIP extraction opens the folder. Linux desktop file managers can extract ZIPs.
Some extractors add an extra outer folder: locate the actual YAML file rather
than relying on a presumed number of nested folders. A Git clone is unnecessary
for this setup; the same runtime files can also be found in the repository.
:::

## Recognise the project root

::: {.project-tree}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
research-methods/
├── README.md
├── environment-student.yml
├── scripts/
│   └── check_setup.py
└── codes/
    └── lecture-1/
        ├── household_saving.py
        ├── project_running.ipynb
        └── data/raw/households.csv
```
:::

Run the installation commands from **`research-methods/`**.

::: {.notes}
This is the student kit root and contains the environment specification. It is
different from codes/lecture-1, which becomes the working project root for the
first classroom exercise. Make that change of starting folder explicit. The
ZIP does not need the slide source, a .git directory, or private configuration.
:::

## Windows · Move the prompt into that folder

Copy the extracted folder's full address from File Explorer.

In **Miniforge Prompt**, use:

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
cd /d "FULL FOLDER ADDRESS"
dir environment-student.yml
```

Replace **FULL FOLDER ADDRESS** with the address you copied; keep the quotes.

::: {.answer}
The directory listing should show **`environment-student.yml`**.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is Windows Command Prompt syntax, as used by Miniforge Prompt, not Bash
or PowerShell syntax. The /d also changes drive if needed. Quotes allow spaces
in a project folder name. The placeholder must be replaced with the actual
path; students should not paste it unchanged. Running from inside a compressed
ZIP or from the lesson subfolder will fail the YAML-file check.
:::

## macOS / Linux · Move Terminal into that folder

In **Terminal**, use:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
cd "FULL FOLDER ADDRESS"
ls environment-student.yml
```

Replace **FULL FOLDER ADDRESS** with the actual extracted folder path.

On macOS you can type `cd `, drag the folder into Terminal, and press Enter.

::: {.answer}
The listing should show **`environment-student.yml`**.
:::

::: {.notes}
The space after cd matters for the drag-and-drop shortcut. If typing manually,
use quotes around paths containing spaces. The exact home directory differs
by person and machine; avoid a hard-coded instructor path. Linux students can
also use their file manager's Open in Terminal action where available, then
check that they are in the folder containing the YAML file.
:::

## Create the course environment · Once

From the folder containing the YAML file:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
conda env create --file environment-student.yml
```

Conda installs **Python 3.12, JupyterLab, ipykernel, pandas, NumPy and Matplotlib**.

::: {.small-note}
Wait until the command finishes and the prompt returns before entering the next command.
:::

::: {.notes}
The environment is named research-methods by the file. No standalone Python
download or separate pip commands are needed. Downloads and solving can take
time; a quiet interval alone is not a reason to cancel. Conda's documented
environment-file command is backwards compatible with this invocation. If the
environment already exists, activate it and check it rather than recreating or
deleting it. Source: https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/stable/commands/env/create.html.
:::

## Activate it · In each new terminal session

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
conda activate research-methods
python --version
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Python 3.12.x
```
:::

The final number may differ. The course environment should use **3.12**.

::: {.notes}
The x stands for the patch version; it is not literal output. The terminal may
display (research-methods) at its prompt after activation. Do not type that
prefix. The base install can use a different Python version. Create the
environment once, activate it whenever starting a new work session. Source:
https://docs.conda.io/projects/conda/en/stable/user-guide/tasks/manage-environments.html.
:::

## Run the installation check

Still in the student project root:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
python scripts/check_setup.py
```

The checker imports packages, finds Git, reads the data and runs the starter script.

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
SETUP CHECK PASSED
```
:::

If you see **`FIX`** lines, use them to ask for help.

::: {.notes}
The displayed success line appears near the end, followed by a reminder to run
the notebook. This checker is supplied in the kit. It does not install software,
write data, or alter configuration. It checks the original income and consumption
inputs, so run it before modifying the lesson example. Passing it does not replace
the browser and notebook check that follows. No network access is needed to run it.
:::

## Run your first Python script

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
cd codes/lecture-1
python household_saving.py
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Monthly saving (EUR): 200
```
:::

::: {.key-idea}
You have run Python on your own computer.
:::

::: {.notes}
The shell starts this step in the student kit root. cd enters the first
lesson folder. The calculation uses synthetic monthly income 1000 and
consumption 800; the script prints saving 200. The CSV is a separate teaching
fixture. No file has been uploaded and the result does not require an agent.
If Python cannot open the script, check the current folder and exact filename.
:::

## Start JupyterLab from the lesson folder

In the same terminal, now inside **`codes/lecture-1`**:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
jupyter lab
```

- Your browser should open JupyterLab.
- Keep the launch terminal open while working.
- If the browser stays closed, use the local URL printed in the terminal.

::: {.small-note}
The browser is the interface to your local JupyterLab session.
:::

::: {.notes}
Official launch instructions: https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started/starting.html.
The URL may include a session token; it should not be posted or included in
help screenshots. The running terminal is serving the notebook and is expected
to stay busy. A local browser page is not a request to upload the project to a
website. Starting from the lesson folder makes its notebook and data visible.
:::

## Open the notebook and check a complete run

1. In JupyterLab, open **`project_running.ipynb`**.
2. Select its **Python 3** kernel if prompted.
3. Choose **Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells…**.
4. Check the outputs, then save the notebook.

::: {.answer}
The file check should be **`True`**. Saving should be **`200`**.
:::

::: {.notes}
The kernel should come from the environment used to launch JupyterLab. Menu
wording can vary slightly by version; select the action that restarts the kernel
and runs every cell in page order. The baseline notebook is unexecuted and has
five code cells. If the file check fails, inspect the working-folder output and
the extracted data path. Do not change the inputs until this baseline passes.
:::

## Next time · Start work in three commands

Open the correct prompt and first enter the **student project root**.

Then run:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
conda activate research-methods
cd codes/lecture-1
jupyter lab
```

::: {.key-idea}
Create the environment **once**. Activate it **for each session**.
:::

::: {.notes}
These commands assume the starting folder contains environment-student.yml.
A fresh terminal does not necessarily start there, so first use the relevant
Windows or macOS/Linux cd step. A terminal already inside lecture-1 should not
repeat the relative cd codes/lecture-1 command. The classroom notebook work
does not require rerunning the environment installer each day.
:::

## Finish a session cleanly

1. Save the notebook and any edited scripts.
2. Return to the terminal where you launched JupyterLab.
3. Press **Ctrl + C** to stop the server; confirm if prompted.

Your files remain on disk for the next session.

::: {.notes}
Closing the browser tab alone may leave the local server running. Saving the
notebook preserves its source and displayed results. The environment remains
installed; there is no reason to remove it at the end of a work session. Do
not close a terminal that is still creating the environment simply because a
download is taking time. This shutdown step refers to the JupyterLab server.
:::

## Install Codex · Desktop route

Codex is available in the **ChatGPT desktop app**.

1. Follow the [official desktop quickstart](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/quickstart).
2. Choose the installer for your operating system and install it.
3. Open the app and sign in with your ChatGPT account.
4. Select **Codex** from the ChatGPT product dropdown.

::: {.notes}
The current OpenAI quickstart documents Codex inside the ChatGPT desktop app.
Use the platform download routes on the next slide. A ChatGPT browser chat does
not by itself provide access to the student's local project. This guide uses
ChatGPT sign-in and does not cover API-key setup. Sources:
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/quickstart and https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth.
:::

## Codex · Choose the desktop installer

| Computer | Official route |
|---|---|
| Windows | [Windows desktop installation guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/windows/windows-app) |
| macOS | [Desktop app download and quickstart](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/app) |
| Linux | [Linux preview: supported systems and packages](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/linux/linux-app) |

On Windows, use the **native Windows** setup with the Windows Python you installed.

::: {.notes}
Windows: the official guide links to the Microsoft Store distribution. On macOS
choose a download compatible with the student's Mac; the IDE route is an
alternative if a compatible build is unavailable. Linux: check the supported
distribution and architecture. There is no need to install WSL for the native
Windows route. Windows-native Conda and a WSL Python installation are different
environments. Sources are the three official links on the slide.
:::

## Codex on Linux · Install the desktop package

From the [official Linux desktop guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/linux/linux-app), choose the package for your distribution and processor.

**Ubuntu / Debian, x64 example:**

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
cd ~/Downloads
sudo apt install ./chatgpt_amd64.deb
```

Use the actual downloaded filename. For ARM64, choose the ARM64 package.

Open **ChatGPT** from Applications, sign in, then select **Codex**.

::: {.notes}
The Linux app is a preview. Check the official supported-distribution list.
Fedora uses its matching RPM and dnf; use the official page instead of this
Debian example. Other systems can use the IDE alternative where supported.
Do not apply these apt commands on Windows or macOS.
Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/linux/linux-app.
:::

## Alternative · Codex in VS Code

Use this route if you already use VS Code or need an alternative to the desktop app.

1. Install [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) for your computer.
2. Follow [OpenAI's Codex extension guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/ide) and its **Install the extension** link.
3. Open the Codex sidebar and choose **Sign in with ChatGPT**.
4. Open the extracted course folder in VS Code.

::: {.small-note}
Choose one Codex route. You do not need both the desktop app and extension.
:::

::: {.notes}
The IDE guide documents a Command Palette fallback: Codex: Open Codex Sidebar.
Use it if the sidebar icon is absent. Sign-in opens a browser and returns to
the client. Notebook work can remain in JupyterLab; the extension is an
alternative agent interface, not a requirement to configure VS Code notebooks.
Sources: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/codex/ide and
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth.
:::

## Open the course folder in Codex

1. In the desktop app, add or open a **local project folder**.
2. Choose the extracted **`research-methods`** folder containing the YAML file.
3. Start a new **Codex** chat in that project.

::: {.key-idea}
Codex should work with the same files you opened in JupyterLab.
:::

Use the app's normal project permissions and review any access requests.

::: {.notes}
Exact button labels may vary. In the IDE route use File > Open Folder instead.
Choose local work on this computer: a cloud workspace does not automatically
use packages installed on the laptop. The selected root includes
scripts/check_setup.py and codes/lecture-1. No GitHub connection is required
to read this local extracted folder.
Source: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/quickstart.
:::

## First Codex message · Read and explain

::: {.exercise}
Read `codes/lecture-1/household_saving.py` in this project.

Explain its inputs, units and calculation. What should it print?

**Do not edit files or install software.**
:::

::: {.answer}
It should explain **`1000 - 800 = 200`**, measured in EUR per month.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a bounded read-only access check. Compare the answer with the actual
script, not just whether it sounds plausible. If the file cannot be located,
check the selected folder. For sign-in or usage problems, record the exact
error for troubleshooting.
:::

## Check which Python Codex uses

Ask Codex to run the checker using the **`research-methods`** environment:

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
conda run --name research-methods python scripts/check_setup.py
```

::: {.key-idea}
Activation in your earlier terminal does not activate a separate Codex session.
:::

If Codex cannot find Conda, run **`conda info --base`** in your working prompt and give it that installation path.

::: {.notes}
Ask it to show the command and full output, without installing packages or
changing files. The command assumes the student project root. Codex may need
the full executable path inside the known Conda installation, especially in
Windows PowerShell. Use that existing installation. The checker does not test
Codex login: the successful agent response and execution are separate checks.
This is a course integration command, not special Codex configuration.
:::

## If installation or activation fails

| What you see | First check |
|---|---|
| `conda` is not found on Windows | Open Miniforge Prompt from Start. |
| `conda` is not found on macOS / Linux | Reopen Terminal after initialization. |
| YAML file cannot be found | Are you in the extracted student project root? |
| Environment already exists | Activate it, then run the setup checker. |
| Downloads or solving fail | Save the first error and ask for setup help. |

::: {.notes}
For a missed Unix shell-initialization step, the official Miniforge instructions
describe using the installed conda by its full path and running conda init.
Do not assume every user's install path or shell. Give that fix individually
when known, rather than asking beginners to paste several competing commands.
Existing environments should be inspected before any update or removal.
:::

## If Python or the notebook fails

| What you see | First check |
|---|---|
| Python reports the wrong version | Activate `research-methods`. |
| A course package is missing | Is the course environment active? |
| `git` is not found | Finish its installation and reopen the prompt. |
| JupyterLab cannot show the notebook | Launch it from `codes/lecture-1`. |
| The data check is `False` | Check the working folder and extracted data folders. |

::: {.notes}
Have students distinguish the terminal environment, notebook kernel and
working folder. The setup checker reports missing imports without changing
anything. On a managed computer a firewall or proxy may affect downloads;
the instructor or local IT should address the actual error. Avoid unrelated
reinstallations as the first response to a path or activation problem.
:::

## Ask for help with evidence

Send the instructor:

- Your **operating system and processor type**.
- The **command** you entered.
- The **first error message**, or the setup checker's **`FIX`** lines.

::: {.small-note}
An error screenshot helps. Keep passwords and Jupyter session tokens out of it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use the normal course contact channel. No new support address is introduced
here. Do not ask students to upload their entire home directory or private
research data. A specific command and its first error is usually enough to
identify the next step. Encourage reporting before class rather than silently
skipping setup. This is ordinary support guidance, not a request to send anything
automatically from the course repository.
:::

## Ready to bring your laptop to class
